content: Previously published reviews have addressed the examinations and tests that should be routinely conducted before initiating contraception. These reviews were utilized to search for evidence regarding the necessary evaluations prior to providing subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA-SC). No new articles were identified, so the analysis relied on the previously published reviews. 1. Tepper NK, Curtis KM, Steenland MW, Marchbanks PA conducted a systematic review on the necessity of blood pressure measurement before initiating hormonal contraception. This was published in Contraception in 2013 (Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 631–638). 2. Tepper NK, Curtis KM, Steenland MW, Marchbanks PA also reviewed the role of physical examinations prior to starting hormonal contraception. This systematic review was published in Contraception in 2013 (Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 650–654). 3. Tepper NK, Steenland MW, Marchbanks PA, Curtis KM performed a systematic review on laboratory screening before initiating contraception. This was published in Contraception in 2013 (Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 645–649). For repeat injections of DMPA-SC, Paulen ME and Curtis KM reviewed the timing for repeat progestogen-only injectables, including depot medroxyprogesterone acetate and norethisterone enanthate. This was published in Contraception in 2009 (Volume 80, Issue 4, Pages 391–408). Regarding the combined contraceptive patch and vaginal ring (CVR), Brahmi D and Curtis KM conducted a systematic review on their initiation. This was published in Contraception in 2013 (Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 524–538). Examinations and tests for the patch and CVR were also addressed in previously published reviews. These reviews were used to search for evidence on routine evaluations before providing the patch or CVR. No new articles were identified, and the analysis relied on the existing reviews. 1. Tepper NK, Curtis KM, Steenland MW, Marchbanks PA reviewed blood pressure measurement before hormonal contraception initiation (Contraception, 2013, Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 631–638). 2. Tepper NK, Curtis KM, Steenland MW, Marchbanks PA reviewed physical examinations before hormonal contraception initiation (Contraception, 2013, Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 650–654). 3. Tepper NK, Steenland MW, Marchbanks PA, Curtis KM reviewed laboratory screening before contraception initiation (Contraception, 2013, Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 645–649). A previously published review exists on dosing errors with combined hormonal contraceptives, including the patch and CVR. This review's search strategy was used to find additional evidence on dosing errors. One new study was identified, which, along with the systematic review, served as the evidence base for this topic. 1. Zapata LB, Steenland MW, Brahmi D, Marchbanks PA, Curtis KM reviewed the effect of missed combined hormonal contraceptives on contraceptive effectiveness (Contraception, 2013, Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 685–700). 2. Dragoman M, Petrie K, Torgal A, Thomas T, Cremers S, Westhoff CL conducted a prospective study on contraceptive vaginal ring effectiveness during six weeks of use in women with normal BMI and obesity (Contraception, 2013, Volume 87, Issue 4, Pages 432–436). Follow-up after patch or CVR initiation was addressed in previously published reviews. These reviews were used to search for evidence on follow-up needs. Three new articles were identified in addition to the published reviews. 1. Steenland MW, Zapata LB, Brahmi D, Marchbanks PA, Curtis KM reviewed appropriate follow-up to detect potential adverse events after initiating select contraceptive methods (Contraception, 2013, Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 611–624). 2. Steenland MW, Zapata LB, Brahmi D, Marchbanks PA, Curtis KM reviewed the effect of follow-up visits or contacts on method continuation and correct use (Contraception, 2013, Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 625–630). 3. Berenson AB, Rahman M conducted a randomized controlled study on two educational interventions to improve adherence to oral contraceptives and condoms (Contraception, 2012, Volume 86, Issue 6, Pages 716–724). 4. Brindis CD, Geierstanger SP, Wilcox N, McCarter V, Hubbard A evaluated a peer provider reproductive health service model for adolescents (Perspectives on Sexual and Reproductive Health, 2005, Volume 37, Issue 2, Pages 85–91). 5. Nisenbaum MG, Melo NR, Giribela CR, Morais TL, Guerra GM, de Angelis K, et al. studied the effects of a contraceptive containing drospirenone and ethinyl estradiol on blood pressure and autonomic tone (European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, 2014, Volume 175, Pages 62–66). For emergency contraception, an unpublished review exists on the initiation of emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs). The search strategy was expanded to include ulipristal acetate ECPs (UPA-ECPs). Two new articles were identified in addition to those summarized in the unpublished review. 1. Rodriguez MI, Gaffield ME authored an unpublished review on how women can take emergency contraceptive pills (available upon request). 2. Glasier A, Cameron ST, Fine P, Logan SJ, Casale W, Van Horn J, et al. conducted a randomized, non-inferiority trial and meta-analysis comparing ulipristal acetate and levonorgestrel for emergency contraception (Lancet, 2010, Volume 375, Issue 9714, Pages 555–562). 3. Fine P, Mathé H, Ginde S, Cullins V, Morfesis J, Gainer E studied ulipristal acetate taken 48–120 hours after intercourse for emergency contraception (Obstetrics & Gynecology, 2010, Volume 115, Issue 2, Pages 257–263). Nausea and vomiting after UPA-ECP use were reviewed by Rodriguez MI, Godfrey EM, Warden M, Curtis KM, focusing on prevention and management (Contraception, 2013, Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 583–589). Resumption or initiation of regular contraception after emergency contraception was reviewed by Salcedo J, Rodriguez MI, Curtis KM, Kapp N (Contraception, 2013, Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 602–604). Appendix 2 details declarations of interest from 58 experts involved in this work. Fourteen experts declared interests related to contraception. The WHO Secretariat and the Guidelines Development Group (GDG) reviewed these declarations. One participant, Anna Glasier, disclosed an academic conflict of interest sufficient to preclude her from participating in deliberations and recommendations related to ulipristal acetate (UPA).
